summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) with network management tools such as SNMP. It covers sparse mode, bidirectional and dense mode. It is meant to replace RFC 2934 in practice.

eli5.summary: This gives network operators a standard set of dials and gauges for checking on and managing multicast routers over SNMP, whichever PIM flavor they run.

questions: how to monitor pim with snmp
which pim modes does the mib support
subtitle: The standard SNMP MIB module for monitoring and configuring PIM multicast routers, for IPv4 and IPv6 alike.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to inspect and configure Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) routers through network management tools. The earlier MIB, RFC 2934, only supported IPv4 and had no support for bidirectional PIM.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5060 defines the PIM-STD-MIB module, rooted at { mib-2 157 }. It is a set of tables and scalar objects covering interfaces, neighbors, multicast state, bidirectional-PIM election, static Rendezvous Points, group mappings and anycast RP sets, plus notifications.
tldr.outcome: It is meant to be preferred over RFC 2934 where the two overlap, but it does not obsolete it. Several writable objects can disturb multicast routing, so SNMPv3 security is recommended.

today: RFC 5060 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes itself as part of the work to obsolete RFC 2934 and says it is to be preferred where the two overlap, while explicitly not obsoleting it.

sections.title: Introduction and What Changed
sections.content:
RFC 5060 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing the Protocol Independent Multicast protocols: PIM-SM (Sparse Mode, RFC 4601), BIDIR-PIM (Bidirectional, RFC 5015) and PIM-DM (Dense Mode, RFC 3973). Managed objects are normally reached with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are defined with SMIv2.

The module reworks the experimental MIB of RFC 2934. The major changes are that it is independent of IP version (RFC 2934 supported only IPv4), supports BIDIR-PIM, keeps only limited support for PIM-DM, drops PIM-SM version 1, no longer depends on the IPv4 Multicast Routing MIB of RFC 2932, and adds configuration of static Rendezvous Points (RPs) and anycast RPs (RFC 4610).
sections.eli5: An older instruction panel only worked for the old kind of addresses. This new panel works with both old and new addresses and has more buttons.

sections.title: The Tables in the Module
sections.content:
The module contains thirteen tables. Several describe the router's own neighborhood: the PIM Interface Table has one row per IP version for each interface running PIM, the PIM Neighbor Table has a row for each PIM neighbor, and the PIM Neighbor Secondary Address Table has a row for each secondary address a neighbor advertises.

Six tables hold multicast routing state: (*,G), (*,G,I), (S,G), (S,G,I), (S,G,rpt) and (S,G,rpt,I). Each has one row per group, or per source and group, and the entries ending in I add the interface for interface-specific state.

The remaining four cover rendezvous and election: the PIM Bidir DF-Election Table (one row per interface for each RP with Designated Forwarder election state), the PIM Static RP Table (one row per range of group addresses that should use a configured RP), the PIM Group Mapping Table (a mapping from a group address prefix to the PIM mode and RP address, whatever the source of the mapping) and the PIM Anycast-RP Set Table (one row per RP within each anycast-RP set the local router belongs to).
sections.eli5: The module is a set of spreadsheets. One lists the router's connections, one lists its neighbors, several list which multicast groups it is tracking, and a few list the meeting points.

sections.title: Textual Conventions: Modes and Mapping Origins
sections.content:
Two textual conventions give names to small sets of values. PimMode says which mode a group is operating in: none (1), ssm (2), asm (3), bidir (4), dm (5) and other (6). A group may have mode none if, for example, it is a link-local or unroutable address.

PimGroupMappingOriginType records how a group mapping was learned: fixed (1) for link-local or unroutable groups, configRp (2) for local static RP configuration, configSsm (3), bsr (4) for the PIM Bootstrap Router mechanism, autoRP (5) for Cisco's Auto-RP, embedded (6) for the Embedded-RP mechanism, and other (7).

Static RP rows also carry a precedence value that feeds the group mapping precedence. If a static RP entry is set to override dynamic configuration, all dynamic RP configuration is overridden whatever the precedence. The RFC says to use precedence only when fine control of static RP behavior on the local router is required.
sections.eli5: Instead of using secret numbers, the module uses labels: how a group is being shared, and how the router found out about its meeting point.

sections.title: Global Timers and Counters
sections.content:
Beyond the tables, the module has scalar objects directly under pim. Two read-write timers mirror values from the PIM-SM specification. pimKeepalivePeriod is the time a router keeps (S,G) state without local membership or join messages, with default 210 seconds. pimRegisterSuppressionTime is how long a Designated Router stops sending Register-encapsulated data to the RP after a Register-Stop message, with default 60 seconds. Both take values from 0 to 65535 seconds.

Other scalars count entries in the state tables and count events, such as pimInvalidRegisterMsgsRcvd and pimRPMappingChangeCount. A set of notification-period objects control how often each notification may be sent. The storage type of these timers is determined by pimDeviceConfigStorageType.
sections.eli5: There are also a few stopwatches you can adjust and a few tally counters that count how often something odd happened.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
The module defines five notifications: pimNeighborLoss (loss of an adjacency with a neighbor), pimInvalidRegister, pimInvalidJoinPrune, pimRPMappingChange and pimInterfaceElection. Each has a matching period object. That object sets the minimum time that must elapse between notifications of its kind, and the maximum value, 65535, means an infinite time, so the notification is never sent.

Each notification also has a counter that increments whenever such a notification would be generated, such as pimRPMappingChangeCount. Operators can therefore poll the counters instead of relying on notifications.
sections.eli5: When something important changes, the router can ring a bell. A setting controls how often it may ring, and a tally counter keeps count even when the bell is off.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects are read-write or read-create and could be used to modify multicast routing behavior in a way that prevents, disrupts or subverts network services. The RFC lists them, including the timers, the interface configuration, the static RP table and the anycast RP set table. Some readable objects may also be sensitive, so access to them should be controlled.

The pimInvalidRegister notification is singled out because it could carry a denial-of-service attack from the data or control plane into the management plane. Three safeguards apply. The notification is disabled by default and needs pimInvalidRegisterNotificationPeriod to be set. The syntax of that object prevents a device from sending it more often than once every 10 seconds. The counter pimInvalidRegisterMsgsRcvd gives equivalent information, and management applications are encouraged to monitor it instead. The same measures apply to pimInvalidJoinPrune, though that risk is less acute.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lack adequate security. Implementers are RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. For IANA, the PIM-STD-MIB module is rooted under the mib-2 subtree and IANA assigned { mib-2 157 } to it.
sections.eli5: Some of the dials can mess up the network if the wrong person turns them, so only trusted people should be allowed to touch them, using the secure version of the control system.
